name: Cryoneuromodulation

lead:
Cryoneuromodulation uses a cold probe, often cooled by nitrous oxide, to temporarily block conduction in a nerve. For wrinkles, the idea is to weaken the small muscles that crease the skin, such as those between the brows, in a way that wears off as the nerve recovers.
It is discussed as a needle-based alternative to botulinum toxin for movement lines. Published work includes animal studies on nerve recovery after focused cold; human cosmetic data are limited.

paras: A clinician applies a probe near a target nerve; coolant expansion forms a small cold zone. Effects are temporary and the nerve typically regenerates over months. In wrinkle contexts this remains investigational.

Nitrous-oxide cooling produces a reversible (second-degree) nerve injury, while much colder agents like liquid nitrogen cause lasting injury. Cold treatment near facial nerves must be precisely targeted.

chain: Cold probe near a facial motor nerve
Softer expression lines until the nerve recovers
angle.text: Proponents propose cold nerve treatment as a toxin-free way to relax muscles behind frown and forehead lines. The effect is temporary by design.

lead: Cryoneuromodulation, also called cryoneurolysis when used for pain, temporarily blocks nerve conduction by freezing a target nerve with a small probe.[1] With nitrous oxide as the coolant (about -88 C), the injury is second-degree: the axon and myelin are disrupted but connective tissue stays intact, so the nerve usually recovers within months.[1]

In cosmetic discussions, the same principle is proposed for facial lines: cooling near the temporal branch of the facial nerve could temporarily weaken the frontalis and glabellar muscles that cause forehead and frown lines.[2] A 2014 rat study found tibial nerve cold treatment temporarily weakened limb function with full nerve regeneration by 16 weeks.[2]
Approved devices such as the iovera system use nitrous oxide and are used for pain relief after surgery.[1]

paras: Pressurised coolant expands at the probe tip and forms an iceball. Nitrous oxide produces reversible axonotmesis, whereas liquid nitrogen produces irreversible injury.[1]

No studies of cosmetic wrinkle treatment in humans have been published. Related research includes a preclinical study of selective focused cold therapy to reduce muscle motility, noting cosmetic relevance,[2] cell-level cryo-neuromodulation device work,[3] and trials in pain contexts; a cited knee pain trial found no robust benefit over sham.[1]
